"Big investors are buying the dip. Retail traders are not"

Last week the S&P 500 had its worst week since April 2025, and BofA’s client data shows exactly who bought it and who ran.

The big money bought. Institutions put in $6.1B, about $4B of it through ETFs, and hedge funds were net buyers for the first time in four weeks.

Retail sold, for the fourth week in a row. They dumped $3.4B of single stocks while still putting $1.4B into ETFs.

$5.3B went into equity ETFs, the 4th-biggest week in BofA’s data, mostly broad US large-cap funds. Tech got bought for the first time in four weeks, and industrials saw their 15th straight week of outflows.

Since the April 2025 tariff shock, retail has been the one catching the falling knife.

This time retail was selling, and Thursday’s crash started with retail buying puts.

So the people who usually panic are the ones who stepped in, and the people who usually step in are the ones who panicked.

I've been a net buyer from Thursday until Tuesday.

When smart money buys what retail is dumping, I pay attention.

Bullish ⚡️

George from 🕹prodmgmt.world@nurijanian
00:34 SGT quoteTech
what is product management, if we break it down to first principles

there is an organization that exists to create value for the market it serves.

to create real value for a market, someone has to figure out what that market needs and design something that solves that need.

the solution must be something the organization can actually build and sell.

it must not conflict with the current strategy. ideally, it should clearly fit the strategy, strengthen it, or even help shape and define the strategy.

- it’s not linear; you take quite a few shots. good stuff takes time.
- it’s heavy on execution and grind, but it also has to be creative and maintain trust.
- experience and product sense matter a lot.
- work used to be done by many people. now maybe not so much, but it still requires others. someone has to lead it.

this function is key in an org, and i still think 1 orchestrator is best here (human or AI, tbc)

otherwise each function pushes into its own corner, and you never reach the bare equilibrium you need to be successful. the product has the wrong components, or gets shipped too late.

(bad product management can happen too. one person, but the wrong one, and you get the same result.)

who should be doing this role?

technically, anyone... assuming they are high-agency, analytical, creative, clear thinker and communicator, low ego, high trust and integrity, work well with others, and ideally have lots of good ideas, experience and/or at least talk to customers all day.

which is probably why companies keep looking.

$ARM

It’s been a while since I’ve taken a closer look at $ARM, but there have been some really interesting developments cooking in the background.

This week Google announced its new TPU 8i Max, the latest in its line of custom AI chips. Like TPU 8t and TPU 8i before it, it runs on Google’s own Arm-based Axion CPUs as the host, so Google’s newest AI chips are all being built around Arm, something the market seems to have overlooked.

Every TPU needs a CPU next to it to feed it data and run the work around it, which means every TPU Google adds pulls more Arm in with it.

Axion also runs Google’s regular cloud servers at up to 2x better price-performance than comparable x86 machines, and AI agent sandboxes run about 30% cheaper on it.

Arm-based servers were already more than 45% of server revenue in Q1, according to IDC, and Arm expects to pass 60% share across the top U.S. clouds by the end of 2026.

Google’s new TPUs are getting all the headlines, but don’t think for a second they’ll rise on their own. Every TPU ships with a CPU, and it’s built on Arm.

Great news for Arm.

Bullish ⚡️

Berkshire Hathaway is making a historic comeback:

Berkshire Hathaway outperformed the S&P 500 by +19.2 percentage points over the 1 month ending Thursday, its largest rolling monthly outperformance since 2010.

This also ranks as the 4th-largest such outperformance in 30 years.

By comparison, its biggest monthly rolling outperformance occurred during the 2008 Financial Crisis, at +29.6 percentage points.

As of Tuesday's close, the performance gap narrowed to +16.9 percentage points, but it still ranked as one of the largest since 1996.

This comes as Berkshire Hathaway's Class B stock has surged +13.2% over the last month, to an all-time high, while the S&P 500 has declined -3.7% over the same period.

To put this into perspective, Berkshire was underperforming the S&P 500 by -14.3 percentage points in May 2026.

Berkshire Hathaway appears strong, even without Warren Buffett as CEO.

$CRWV $NBIS $IREN $NVDA

I went through CoreWeave’s Q3 report and call line by line, and it’s the strongest neocloud print I’ve seen this year.

Revenue grew 168% to $3.66B, ahead of estimates, and adjusted operating income hit $379M against guidance of $200M to $260M.

Full-year guidance went up to $13.0B–$13.3B, and CoreWeave expects to exit 2026 at a $20B–$21B revenue run rate.

Demand is 10x available capacity through 2027, and every bit of 2028 capacity offered so far is already sold.

Backlog hit $132.5B, up 138% in a year. The part due within 24 months more than doubled to ~$48B.

Prices went up ~25% in July and another 10% after. Short-term capacity now sells for $40M+ per MW a year, and older Ampere and Hopper GPUs repriced 30–50% higher.

The interest bill everyone is worried about went from 25x operating income in Q1 to 2.2x in Q3. Over 75% of capex through 2027 is backed by investment-grade and enterprise customers, and management expects contracted cash flow to repay the debt.

130,000 GPUs come off contract in 2027 and 170,000 more in 2028. Re-signed at today’s prices, that’s close to $10B of run-rate revenue with zero new capex.

You simply are not bullish enough on AI compute.

Central banks are aggressively buying the dip in gold.

We shouldn’t really hike into December let alone 50 bps.

Oil just had its biggest weekly drop since 2020. Stocks just had their worst week since April 2025.

CPI, is a rearview mirror, Yes, October was hot: 0.4% headline, 0.3% core. But core is running around 2.7% a year, right around its 40-year average. One ugly print is one data point, and the Fed is supposed to wait for the trend.

You don't hike into a supply shock.

Higher rates don't pump a single extra barrel of oil. They just break whatever was already wobbling.

And where was all this urgency in 2021, when inflation hit 7% and the Fed spent most of the year calling it transitory?

A 50bp move is for emergencies. Nothing here is an emergency.

If it were up to me, they wouldn't hike at all in anticipation of what’s to come.

Make it make sense please, we need to accelerate not slow down this growth machine.

Our direct experience with Nvidia, never shared before:

22 months ago, we published the below analysis raising concerns that Nvidia's AI chips were potentially being routed to China through Singapore.

Less than 24 hours later, Nvidia's Head of PR contacted us, directly addressing our analysis. Their message to us is included below.

At the time, in the previous 3 quarters, $17.4 billion of Nvidia's revenue came from Singapore versus $11.6 billion from China.

Furthermore, at the time, the US had ~5,375 data centers, China had 448, and Singapore had just 99. The numbers just did not add up. You can read our full analysis below.

Nvidia's PR team sent us the following message:

"The revenue associated with Singapore does not indicate diversion to China. Our public filings report 'bill to' not 'ship to' locations of our customers. Many of our customers have business entities in Singapore and use those entities for products destined for the US and the West. We insist that our partners comply with all applicable laws, and if we receive any information to the contrary, act accordingly. Our last 10-Q noted: 'most shipments associated with Singapore revenue were to locations other than Singapore and shipments to Singapore were insignificant.'"

Fast forward to today.

According to new reports, Nvidia, $NVDA, CEO Jensen Huang's relationship with a suspected Chinese spy helped facilitate at least $7.5 billion in Nvidia chip shipments to Chinese companies through a network spanning China and Singapore.

The reported shipments date back to 2023 and involved ~240,000 advanced Nvidia AI chips.

These allegations remain under investigation, and it is not yet established whether the shipments were connected to the revenue discrepancies we highlighted 22 months ago.

Nvidia maintains that it has no reason to believe US national security or company secrets were compromised.

But the overlap between these new allegations and the questions we raised in January 2025, along with Nvidia's response to us at the time, is noteworthy.

We stand by our view that Jensen Huang is likely to remain CEO of Nvidia and will continue to be an integral figure in the AI Revolution.

We expect more on this soon.

On the Nvidia situation:

Nvidia, $NVDA, is now down another -7% today and -12% since the Jensen Huang affair situation began.

At this point, the market is pricing in two major potential headwinds.

First, the growing possibility that Jensen Huang will be removed as CEO.

Second, possibility that sensitive Nvidia technology or information was compromised.

Are these scenarios possible? Sure, but we believe both remain unlikely, with less than a 20% probability.

Nvidia's stock is now down -32% in just 24 trading days, erasing -$1.8 trillion in market cap, with over one-third of these losses coinciding with the Jensen Huang controversy.

We believe Huang remains an integral part of Nvidia's future and the broader AI Revolution, and this week's events will not derail the broader thesis.

As the dust settles and uncertainty begins to fade, we expect bargain hunters to step in.

The fundamental AI investment thesis remains intact.

Why Nvidia is continuing to take a further hit today...

- The Information reported that a network linked to Alice Huang allegedly facilitated at least $7.5 billion in Nvidia chip shipments to Chinese companies, involving roughly 240,000 AI chips, including models restricted from sale in China. This would basically mean Nvidia has sold to China when they weren't supposed to.

- Bloomberg reported that Nvidia's inventory figures provided to U.S. authorities undercounted approximately 50,000 AI chips worth billions of dollars sold to Megaspeed through hardware partners. Nvidia later claimed the hardware was located at additional warehouses but did not provide a detailed accounting. Basically, if those 50K chips aren't accounted for...could they have gone to China?

Both those headlines broke over the past 24 hours as Nvidia is now at a $4.02T marketcap, losing over $1T in value over the past month.

United are starting over now that Carrick is on the verge of being sacked

If you look at CW laser ASPs for AI data centers, the pricing differences are pretty substantial:

70mW: ~$3–4
100mW: ~$4–6 (Source Photonics channel checks).

With some premiums apparently going up to $7-$9 range with the recent shortage for pluggables.

120–150mW NPO: ~$15–20
350mW UHP CW: ~$40 (Nomura)
400mW UHP CW for NPO/CPO: ~$50–75 (Mizuho)

With former communication laser chips going from 20-50 cents.

The pricing and gross margins of these players go up with each architectural shift (60%+ for CPO lasers).

And go up even more depending how far down the stack you go (selling ELSFP was ~2.5x revenue content)

In terms of how I see the landscape now:

- $COHR is probably the best risk adjusted laser player now, for people who don't like uncertainty. Their new $20B LTA is very substantial.

- $LITE pretty negative now given the valuation overhang from $MRVL acquisition. Operationally very opsitive.

- $AAOI has extreme demand visibility (likely $6-$9B in new LTAs from just 1 quarter), but credible execution uncertainty.

They've also been focusing on pluggables + bottlenecked by DSPs, rather focusing on UHP CPO laser merchant markets.

But I think if markets see a new $5B-$7B LTA that they're in late stage discussion for... and see the $4.4B MC. Pretty sure that's a catalyst for recovery.

The demand doesn't disappear but timeline shifts back a few months.

AOI also signaled DSP as the main bottleneck, last quarter it was TIAs, so other different component players that are interesting.

- $SIVE has extreme capacity expansion (300m laser capacity targeted in total).

The economic implications that they won't disclose are likely enormous relative to their MC, even if they sell $3 70mW lasers to China pluggable players.

But there's a qualification uncertainty to fill the gap,

Habesha Tech Bro @HabeshaTechBro · 10 Nov 2026, 14:22 SGT
One nuance worth adding for the semi specialists reading the $AAOI section:

The 720M to 1.44B annual diode figure off the 180,000/year Yunnan Germanium 4-inch wafer contract reflects gross standard pluggable die candidates. Once you apply real-world III-V epitaxy,facet-coating, and 5,000-hour burn-in yields (~45% to 55% net known-good dies), factor in dual-use export license buffers, and account for the ~5x die-area penalty on 300mW to 400mW CPO cavities, $AAOI's net shippable output scales toward ~180M to 300M+ high-speed lasers per year as Texas Phase 2 ramps.

Roughly 80M to 95M of those net dies get absorbed internally just feeding $AAOI's 1M/month transceiver target, leaving ~100M to 200M+ merchant diodes for external buyers inside a 650M to 1B+ combined scale-out and scale-up market. Even if both $AAOI and $SIVE hit full utilization in 2028, merchant Western supply stays structurally short.

Lukas Kafka @Kafka7invest · 10 Nov 2026, 05:06 SGT
$SNAP
Open Letter to Evan Spiegel @evanspiegel
Chief Executive Officer, Snap Inc.

November 9, 2026

Evan Spiegel
Chief Executive Officer
Snap Inc.
3000 31st Street
Santa Monica, CA 90405

Dear Mr. Spiegel,
As a long-term shareholder of Snap Inc., I write to respectfully urge a significant increase in the company’s share repurchase program. While Snap has made meaningful progress in revenue growth, profitability, and free cash flow generation, the ongoing dilution from stock-based compensation (SBC) continues to exert a material negative drag on per-share value for owners.

I specifically request that quarterly share buybacks exceed the dilution caused by SBC each quarter. Doing so would produce a net reduction in the total share count on both a quarterly and annual basis. With common shares outstanding plus shares underlying stock-based awards currently exceeding 1.93 billion and continuing to grow, systematically shrinking the share base is essential to translating operating improvements into lasting shareholder returns.

Reducing shares outstanding directly improves earnings per share (EPS) and free cash flow per share. The same absolute earnings and free cash flow are divided among fewer shares, mechanically increasing these key metrics and compounding value for remaining shareholders over time. This approach also strengthens the balance sheet’s efficiency without requiring incremental operating improvements beyond those already underway.

Warren Buffett has long argued that companies should repurchase shares when they trade below intrinsic value relative to their financial fundamentals. At current prices, Snap appears undervalued relative to its growing free cash flow, user base, and improving margins. Deploying capital into buybacks at these levels would be accretive, increase ownership for long-term holders, and align capital allocation with the interests of patient shareholders—precisely the framework Buffett endorses.

I urge the Board and management to adopt a disciplined, ongoing buyback policy that prioritizes net share count reduction. Such a commitment would demonstrate confidence in Snap’s intrinsic value and reward those who have invested for the long term.

Thank you for your consideration.

Sincerely,
A Concerned Long-Term Shareholder
Snap Inc.

James E. Thorne @DrJStrategy · 10 Nov 2026, 08:30 SGT
The Data Center Buildout Is Not Dead

The Senate’s 73-25 vote to advance the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act undercuts the claim that rapid data center expansion is politically finished.

With White House support and President Trump publicly backing the measure as a way to unleash energy production and protect ratepayers, the bill both raises costs for operators and clears the largest practical obstacle to new capacity: the inability to build power and transmission on a workable timeline.

Under the legislation, large loads of roughly 20 megawatts or more must cover the full incremental cost of the generation, transmission, and distribution upgrades built to serve them. Ratepayers are shielded from cost shifting, and states gain additional tools to impose collateral or other requirements. Modeling suggests this could meaningfully increase the retail power price faced by data centers and add roughly 10 percent to the annualized cost of a gigawatt-scale facility. Those numbers are real, and some marginal projects will be repriced or delayed.

They are not fatal. The same bill shortens federal environmental reviews, limits the window for legal challenges, strengthens project certainty, and expands federal transmission siting authority after a defined state review period. The binding constraint on data center growth has not been the willingness of capital to fund servers; it has been the multi-year wait for reliable power. Faster permitting of generation and transmission addresses that bottleneck directly.

Higher power costs and clearer cost allocation will push some developers toward co-located generation or more selective site selection. That is an adjustment, not a shutdown. The combination of ratepayer protections, accelerated infrastructure deployment, and explicit Trump administration support is more likely to sustain the buildout than to end it. The political signal is that Washington is prepared to let the projects proceed, provided the incremental costs fall on the operators rather than on everyone else.

good point by Matt, perhaps obvious for PMs

I like to transition my /opportunity workflow straight into grilling so that the whole thread from “these are the problems people have, let’s solve this branch” to “here’s how we solve this” is contextualized
Matt Pocock @mattpocockuk · 10 Nov 2026, 04:22 SGT
One tip to improve your grilling

Instead of talking about the 'what', try explaining more of the 'why'.

BAD: "I want to build an analytics panel for admins with graphs and filters"

GOOD: "Admins can't currently see an overview of the important data in the app"

If you start by explaining your proposed solution, the agent will stick to it. It'll assume all the important stuff is settled, and just grill you on implementation.

But if you describe the problem, you'll give the agent license to be more creative.

You'll end up with a much deeper, better conversation.

The scale of Big Tech's AI future financial obligations is extraordinary:

Alphabet, $GOOGL, Meta, $META, Anthropic, Microsoft, $MSFT, Amazon, $AMZN, Oracle, $ORCL, and Nvidia, $NVDA, have disclosed a combined $4.49 trillion in off-balance-sheet obligations.

These include future lease payments that have not yet commenced, data-center commitments, equipment purchases, and other contractual obligations.

Alphabet accounts for the largest amount, at $1.08 trillion, followed by Anthropic, at $865 billion, and Meta, at $810 billion.

By comparison, their combined on-balance-sheet obligations total just $758 billion, consisting of long-term debt and existing lease liabilities.

This means off-balance-sheet commitments are nearly 6 times larger than their on-balance-sheet obligations.

In total, these 7 tech companies face ~$5.25 trillion in combined financial obligations.

The AI infrastructure race is facing enormous future financial commitments.

In fact, the AI trade, and the market's rally as a whole, appears to be broadening.

Innovation is at an all-time high and markets know it.

This is the most resilient market in history.
